answers.notes:
Similar to the Prep Unit, I need to teach a PCMS focus for the first four lessons, but with a slightly higher degree of application: 

PCMS / SWPBS Focus
Week 2
Classroom Expectations

LI: To behave safely and kindly in our specialist room.


Purpose from PCMS: When students know exactly what behaviour is expected of them, they are more likely to demonstrate these behaviours in the classroom. Teachers establish clear, consistent guidelines for conduct, which helps create a structured and positive learning environment.

Expectations to be taught:
Mini lesson / Task / Pack up
Toilet / drink
Out of bounds areas
Week 3
Classroom Procedures & Routines

LI: To follow routines so everyone can learn safely and calmly

Lesson starts off, do roll then practice transition to the basketball court during the first 10 mins of the lesson

Cut off class 10 mins early and heavy focus on transitions.

Purpose from PCMS: Procedures are the process for how things are done. When taught to fluency, they help students to form routines to efficiently and smoothly accomplish tasks. Teachers should implement these procedures because they minimise confusion and maximise instructional time.

Routines to be taught:
In-class transitions
Arriving & departing
Swapping over with other Specialists
Workbook expectations
Placement of personal belongings 
Week 4
Encouraging Expected Behaviour

Trial in term 1 working towards a Stamp Target

LI: To show behaviours that help everyone learn safely and happily in our specialist room.

Purpose from PCMS: To effectively recognise and encourage students when they display expected behaviours and to create a positive school environment where learning flourishes.

Expected behaviours to be taught/acknowledged:
Revise expectations from first week
Showing Kindness, Resilience and Responsibility
Classroom acknowledgement system (e.g. stamps for positive behaviours)
Give feedback at a 4:1 positive to corrective ratio (9:1 positive to corrective for students who may have experienced trauma)
Week 5
Discouraging Inappropriate Behaviour

Develop a pack for each Specialist class (Senior to Junior School) for students to reflect when removed.

LI: To respond calmly and respectfully when things go wrong in our Specialist room.

Purpose from PCMS: Specific corrective feedback is a necessary component of the learning process as students need to know when they have made an error and be redirected to the expected behaviour. Additionally, timely and constructive feedback prevents the escalation of negative behaviours, maintaining a conducive learning environment for all students.

School-wide sequence for minor behaviours:
Remind: A discreet reminder of the expected behaviour (1:1)
Redirect: Offer specific support or options to help the student re-engage (no more than two strategies)
Relocate: Move to a different seat or different class in PLT if behaviour continues, with follow-up reflection and communication as required

Year 1/2 - I show you and you help me notice what we are doing.
Model and then ask students to describe what they saw.

Suggested CIC: “You already know how to learn in your classroom, but what might be different here?”

Reflection: Pair-Share: One thing we did today that helped us learn.
Model to students the steps for individual classroom routines. Students describe steps out loud. Repeat 2 or 3 times. Ask students to describe how it felt.

Suggested CIC: List each step on a card. Students uncover steps one at a time and put them in order.

Reflection: Students say one step of the routine aloud.
State behaviour and why it matters.
Teacher model plus a student helper.
Quick rehearsal during routine.
Students describe what positive behaviour looked like.

Suggested CIC: What’s one time you were kind, responsible or resilient this week - even outside school?

Reflection: Students finish the sentence: “I helped our room learn when I…”
Quick revision of positive behaviours.
Show what a calm response to a reminder / redirect looks and sounds like. Practise saying kind phrases (e.g. “Okay, I’ll try again”).

Suggested CIC:
What do athletes/musicians/artists do when they make a mistake during a game/performance/etc? Do they stop playing or try again?

How Remind, Redirect, Relocate looks:
Remind: Quiet cue about the expectation.
Redirect: Students try again with teacher support or a simple option.
Relocate: Change of seat with a short reset.

Reflection: Students describe one moment they fixed a mistake calmly.

directions.title: Sound Makers
directions.big_idea: The material you choose changes the sound your instrument makes.

lisc.intention: To design and make a sound maker, using what we know about vibrations, pitch and volume.
criteria: explain that sound is made when something vibrates
change a sound to be higher or lower, louder or softer
choose a material for my sound maker and say why it suits the sound

pairing.how: Students need to know that sound comes from vibrations, and that pitch and volume can change, to choose materials for a sound maker. The materials they choose (card, foil, paper plate, straws, sticks) decide how it vibrates and sounds, so the design cannot be done without the Science. A step card showing how to play it brings in a small algorithm.

built_in.how: Students predict whether a change will make the sound higher or lower before testing.
Students make their sound maker safely with the craft materials.
Students choose the sound maker they prefer and say why.
Students order cards to show the steps, with a repeat, for playing their sound maker and for a classroom routine.
Students record their sound maker on an iPad and add it to a Book Creator page.

assessment.title: Observation checklist
assessment.how: Tick the class list against the three success criteria while students test their sound makers.

assessment.title: Book Creator page
assessment.how: One page per pair with a photo, a voice recording of the sound and one sentence about the material.

assessment.title: Sound maker showcase
assessment.how: Pairs play and explain their sound maker to another pair while James listens in.

arc.title: Safe and Kind in Our Room
arc.summary: PCMS Classroom Expectations: mini lesson, task and pack up, toilet and drink, out of bounds areas. Practise the pack up cue as a listening game.

arc.title: Routines We Can Follow
arc.summary: PCMS Procedures and Routines: roll, then practise the move to the basketball court, arriving and departing, swapping with other Specialists. Class finishes 10 minutes early. A sound cue starts each transition.

arc.title: Kind, Resilient, Responsible
arc.summary: PCMS Encouraging Expected Behaviour: revise expectations, name kindness, resilience and responsibility, and start the stamp target trial.

arc.title: Try Again Calmly
arc.summary: PCMS Discouraging Inappropriate Behaviour: what Remind, Redirect and Relocate look and sound like, ordered on cards, and a calm response.

arc.title: Sound Is Shaking
arc.summary: Feel, see and hear vibrations with sticks, foil and plates. Sound needs something that shakes.

arc.title: High, Low, Loud, Soft
arc.summary: Change pitch and volume by changing length, size and force, and predict the result first.

arc.title: Build a Sound Maker
arc.summary: Choose materials, build, test and improve a sound maker for a chosen sound.

arc.title: Sound Maker Showcase
arc.summary: Play, record and share the sound maker, with a step card for how to play it.

resources.why: Straws, sticks, plates, card and skewers become the sound makers.
Foil and baking paper as vibrating surfaces to compare.
Pebbles and shells as shakers and beaters.
Each pair shows and explains their sound maker.

connections.how: Students listen to and describe sounds, such as loud and soft or high and low, and link them to rhythm and music.
The first four lessons build the safe, kind habits of a shared room, and moving and listening together link to the wellbeing and movement students already practise.

pedagogy.how: Lessons 1 to 4 teach expectations, routines, encouragement and calm responses, with a sound cue starting each routine.
Students plan, build, test and improve a sound maker for a chosen sound.
Vibrate, pitch and volume are taught and used each lesson.
Asking what an athlete or musician does after a mistake opens the calm response lesson, and a mystery sound opens Lesson 5.

backbone: Teach vibrate, pitch and volume explicitly with a worked example before students build.
Retrieve the PCMS routines at the start of each science lesson so the habits stay fresh.
Predict, test, then compare, so students check ideas against what they hear.
Give feedback against the three success criteria while students test their builds.
flair: Open the unit with a mystery sound behind a screen.
Let each pair name their sound maker.
End with a quiet, careful listening parade around the room.
Use a sound to start and stop each transition so the room itself becomes the lesson.

directions.title: Sound Detectives
directions.big_idea: Different materials carry or block sound, and we can find out which with a fair test.

lisc.intention: To investigate how sound travels and how different materials change what we hear.
criteria: explain that sound is made when something vibrates
predict which material will make a sound quieter, then test it fairly
use our results to say which material suits a quiet space

pairing.how: The design question is which material makes the best quiet reading corner, and answering it means testing how materials change volume. Students use what they know about vibrations and volume to read the test, and the properties of each material (soft, hard, thick, thin) become the evidence for the choice.

built_in.how: Students predict which material will make the sound quietest.
Groups follow the same steps in order for every test.
Students sort results into a table of pictures and find the pattern.
Students compare results with their prediction and ask a new question.
Students show test results as pictures and numbers and look for a pattern.
The test method is written as ordered steps with a repeat for each material, the same way the PCMS routines are shown.

assessment.title: Quick prediction check
assessment.how: Hands up or dots on a class chart before and after the test.

assessment.title: Results page
assessment.how: Each group's table of pictures, checked against the success criteria.

assessment.title: Book Creator recommendation
assessment.how: One page per pair with a photo and a recorded sentence saying which material they recommend and why.

arc.title: Sound Is Shaking
arc.summary: Find out what makes sound by feeling and watching things vibrate.

arc.title: Quiet or Loud?
arc.summary: Predict which materials make a sound quieter, then test the same sound behind each one.

arc.title: Fair Test Results
arc.summary: Record results as pictures, sort them, find the pattern and compare with predictions.

arc.title: Quiet Corner Recommendation
arc.summary: Use the evidence to recommend a material, and record it in Book Creator.

resources.why: Pebbles in a tub give the same sound for every test.
Card, paper and plates as test materials.
Foil and baking paper as test materials.
Plasticine as a soft test material.

connections.how: Students listen closely to loud and soft sounds and describe them.
Understanding that loud noise can bother others links to caring for a shared space.

pedagogy.how: Lessons 1 to 4 teach expectations, routines, encouragement and calm responses.
Students follow a guided fair test with the same steps for every material.
Each science lesson opens by recalling vibrate, pitch and volume.
Pictures of the tests and results keep the words to a minimum.

backbone: Model one complete fair test before groups run their own.
Keep the test method identical each time to limit what students juggle.
Retrieve the key words at the start of each lesson.
Check predictions before and after each test and tie feedback to the success criteria.
flair: Give each group detective roles and a case file.
Hide a ticking sound in a tub and ask which material hides it best.
Let the class vote on the quiet corner they would most like to sit in.

directions.title: Sound Signals
directions.big_idea: A sound can be a signal, and a signal follows steps that a person or a computer can follow.

lisc.intention: To use what we know about sound to build a sound game that follows steps.
criteria: explain that sound is made when something vibrates
choose a high or low, loud or soft sound that fits a job
put steps in order, with a repeat, so a game or routine works

pairing.how: Students record sounds made with different materials and must pick the right pitch and volume for each job in their sound game, such as a low loud sound for stop and a high soft sound for go. The material decides the sound, so the Science informs every choice in the build. Digital Technologies carries the making: ordered steps, repeats and a digital system that plays the sounds.

built_in.how: Students predict which sound will best suit each job.
Students draw their sound game layout before building it.
Students use a Makey Makey, a computer and speakers as input and output.
Students decide what a sound signal should tell someone in the room.
Students order cards for the routines in Lessons 1 to 4, then plan a sound sequence with a repeat.

assessment.title: Step cards
assessment.how: Check each pair's ordered cards for the sound sequence with a repeat.

assessment.title: Game demonstration
assessment.how: Pairs play their game to another pair while James uses a checklist against the success criteria.

assessment.title: Book Creator page
assessment.how: One page per pair with a photo of the game and a recorded sentence about which sound they chose and why.

arc.title: Choose the Sound

arc.title: Build the Sound Game

resources.why: Touch pads trigger the recorded sounds.
Record the sounds and take photos.
Pages to show and explain the game.
Foil touch pads and a vibrating surface for recordings.
Card and sticks for the pads and sound makers.

connections.how: Students listen to, describe and choose sounds, and play them in a pattern like a rhythm.
Following routines and signals together links to the safe, kind habits of a shared space.

pedagogy.how: Lessons 1 to 4 teach routines as ordered steps that students can follow and name.
James models ordering the steps of a routine and a sound sequence before students try.
Pairs build the game with prompts and checks along the way.
Step cards and pictures replace long instructions.

backbone: Use the same step cards for routines and for the game so the idea of an ordered sequence transfers.
Model building one touch pad and one sound before pairs do their own.
Retrieve vibrate, pitch and volume at the start of each lesson.
Check understanding with the step cards before the build begins.
flair: Let the class vote on the sound that means stop.
Run a freeze game where a pair's game controls the room.
Check the Makey Makey count and which devices they plug into before planning pairs.

choices.notes: I really need the first four lessons to be very engaging with a little more subtlety around the PCMS stuff, but still clearly evident.
